items.name: Local data attached to a depth zero cuspidal π
items.statement: Let π = c-Ind_{J_π}^G λ_π be an irreducible cuspidal depth zero representation of a classical group G (G is not the split two-dimensional special orthogonal group SO(1,1) ≅ GL_1; E7), with J_π the normalizer of a standard maximal parahoric subgroup J°_{N_1,N_2}, and λ_π|_{J°_{N_1,N_2}} containing an irreducible representation λ°_π inflated from an irreducible cuspidal representation τ_π ≃ τ_π^{(1)} ⊗ τ_π^{(2)} of the reductive quotient 𝒢°_{N_1,N_2} ≃ 𝒢^{(1)}_{N_1} × 𝒢^{(2)}_{N_2}. For i = 1, 2 there is a unique conjugacy class (s_i) in 𝒢^{(i),*}_{N_i} such that τ_π^{(i)} ∈ ℰ(𝒢^{(i)}_{N_i}, s_i); its characteristic polynomial is ∏_P P(X)^{a_P^{(i)}}, the product over irreducible k_F/k_o-self-dual monic P ∈ k_F[X], with a_P^{(i)} satisfying (7.2); so there are integers m_P^{(i)} ⩾ 0 with: if k_F ≠ k_o or P(X) ≠ (X ± 1) then a_P^{(i)} = ½ m_P^{(i)}(m_P^{(i)} + 1); if k_F = k_o and P(X) = (X ± 1) one writes m_+^{(i)} = m_{(X−1)}^{(i)}, m_−^{(i)} = m_{(X+1)}^{(i)}, satisfying (7.2).
items.note: No atlas stage or library declaration covers this: SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups stops at SR.0–SR.6 (smooth category, Hecke algebras, induction/compact induction, admissibility, Satake, GL_n families, finiteness) with no types, covers, depth-zero/Morris data, reducibility points or L-packets for classical groups; no Tau Ceti roadmap treats finite groups of Lie type, Deligne–Lusztig theory or Lusztig series. Inputs: Morris's description of depth zero cuspidals (§3), Lusztig's Jordan decomposition and classification of cuspidal unipotent representations ([32], §7, (7.2)). This parametrisation by the integers m_P^{(i)} is the basic datum for all of §§8–9. Scope (FIX-RT-PAPER-LUST-STEVENS-20, RT-PAPER-LUST-STEVENS-20/5): the local data and the compact-induction description of π used here exclude split SO(1,1) (E7); the paper's §7 likewise excludes SO_2^+ over the finite field, so this case is deferred.

items.name: Remark 8.2: the 'right' trivial group
items.statement: If N_i = N_i^{an} = 0 (i = 1 or 2) the group 𝒢^{(i)}_{N_i} is trivial but is interpreted as: a trivial symplectic group if G is symplectic; a trivial special orthogonal group if G is special orthogonal; a trivial unitary group if G is unramified unitary; and, if G is ramified unitary, a trivial symplectic group if ε = (−1)^i and a trivial special orthogonal group otherwise. If the group is trivial symplectic the characteristic polynomial of s_i is X − 1; in the other cases it is the constant polynomial 1.
items.note: No atlas stage or library declaration covers this: SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups stops at SR.0–SR.6 (smooth category, Hecke algebras, induction/compact induction, admissibility, Satake, GL_n families, finiteness) with no types, covers, depth-zero/Morris data, reducibility points or L-packets for classical groups; no Tau Ceti roadmap treats finite groups of Lie type, Deligne–Lusztig theory or Lusztig series. Convention needed so that the counting identities of §§8.1–8.3 hold uniformly (e.g. a_+ = 1, m_+ = 0 for the trivial symplectic factor).

items.name: Finite-field datum of a depth zero self-dual cuspidal ρ of GL_n(F)
items.statement: For ρ a self-dual irreducible cuspidal depth zero representation of some GL_n(F), there is a unique self-dual irreducible cuspidal representation τ_ρ of GL_n(k_F) such that ρ contains the inflation λ_ρ of τ_ρ to GL_n(𝔬_F). Then τ_ρ lies in the Lusztig series of some conjugacy class in GL_n(k_F) with irreducible self-dual characteristic polynomial Q = Q_ρ of degree n.
items.note: No atlas stage or library declaration covers this: SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups stops at SR.0–SR.6 (smooth category, Hecke algebras, induction/compact induction, admissibility, Satake, GL_n families, finiteness) with no types, covers, depth-zero/Morris data, reducibility points or L-packets for classical groups; no Tau Ceti roadmap treats finite groups of Lie type, Deligne–Lusztig theory or Lusztig series. Green's classification [18] of cuspidals of GL_n(k_F) and depth-zero types for GL_n. The two self-dual members ρ, ρ' of an inertial class share Q_ρ; this indexes the sum in (8.1) by self-dual polynomials P.

items.name: Hecke parameters and reducibility points for Q ≠ X ± 1 or k_F ≠ k_o
items.statement: Suppose k_F ≠ k_o or Q(X) ≠ (X ± 1) (so either n > 1 or G is an unramified unitary group). Then f_i = f_{τ_ρ ⊗ τ_π^{(i)}} = (2m_Q^{(i)} + 1) n/2, and from (5.1) the reducibility points are {±s_π(ρ), ±s_π(ρ')} = {±(m_Q^{(1)} + m_Q^{(2)} + 1)/2, ±(m_Q^{(1)} − m_Q^{(2)})/2}. One of these is an integer and the other a half-integer, and ⌊s_π(ρ)²⌋ + ⌊s_π(ρ')²⌋ = ((m_Q^{(1)} + m_Q^{(2)} + 1)/2)² + ((m_Q^{(1)} − m_Q^{(2)})/2)² − ¼ = a_Q^{(1)} + a_Q^{(2)}.

Uses §§7.6–7.7 (finite Hecke algebra parameters via Lusztig's tables) and (5.1) (Blondel [4, Prop. 3.12]: reducibility of I(ρ,π,s) forces Re s ∈ {±(f_1 ± f_2)/(2n)}). Arithmetic checked: squares sum to a_Q^{(1)} + a_Q^{(2)} + ¼.

items.name: (8.1) for unramified unitary groups
items.statement: If G is an unramified unitary group, Σ_{ρ ∈ 𝒜^σ_{[0]}(F)} ⌊s_π(ρ)²⌋ n_ρ = Σ_P (a_P^{(1)} + a_P^{(2)}) deg(P) = (2N_1 + N_1^{an}) + (2N_2 + N_2^{an}) = 2N + N^{an} = N_Ĝ.

Immediate from the previous item since every P falls in the generic case.

items.name: Symplectic case, Q = X − 1
items.statement: Let G be symplectic, Q(X) = X − 1, so ρ, ρ' are the trivial character and the unramified character of order 2; write m_Q^{(i)} = m_+^{(i)}. Since both 𝒢^{(i)}_{N_i} are symplectic, f_i = (2m_+^{(i)} + 1), with reducibility points {±s_π(ρ), ±s_π(ρ')} = {±(m_+^{(1)} + m_+^{(2)} + 1), ±(m_+^{(1)} − m_+^{(2)})}; thus ⌊s_π(ρ)²⌋ + ⌊s_π(ρ')²⌋ = (m_+^{(1)} + m_+^{(2)} + 1)² + (m_+^{(1)} − m_+^{(2)})² = a_+^{(1)} + a_+^{(2)} − 1.

Checked with a_+ = 2(m_+² + m_+) + 1 (odd special orthogonal dual).

items.name: Symplectic case, Q = X + 1
items.statement: Let G be symplectic, Q(X) = X + 1, so ρ, ρ' are the (tamely) ramified characters of order 2; write m_Q^{(i)} = m_−^{(i)}. Then f_i = 2m_−^{(i)}, with reducibility points {±s_π(ρ), ±s_π(ρ')} = {±(m_−^{(1)} ± m_−^{(2)})}; thus ⌊s_π(ρ)²⌋ + ⌊s_π(ρ')²⌋ = (m_−^{(1)} + m_−^{(2)})² + (m_−^{(1)} − m_−^{(2)})² = a_−^{(1)} + a_−^{(2)}.

Checked with a_− = 2m_−².

items.name: (8.1) for symplectic groups
items.note: No atlas stage or library declaration covers this: SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups stops at SR.0–SR.6 (smooth category, Hecke algebras, induction/compact induction, admissibility, Satake, GL_n families, finiteness) with no types, covers, depth-zero/Morris data, reducibility points or L-packets for classical groups; no Tau Ceti roadmap treats finite groups of Lie type, Deligne–Lusztig theory or Lusztig series. The −1 comes from the Q = X − 1 case.

items.name: Ramified unitary case, Q = X − 1
items.statement: Let G be ramified unitary, with 𝒢^{(1)}_{N_1} symplectic and 𝒢^{(2)}_{N_2} orthogonal (otherwise exchange 1 and 2), Q(X) = X − 1, m_+^{(i)} in place of m_Q^{(i)}. Then f_1 = 2m_+^{(1)} + 1 and f_2 = 2m_+^{(2)} + 1 if N_2^{an} = 1, f_2 = 2m_+^{(2)} otherwise. The reducibility points {±s_π(ρ), ±s_π(ρ')} are {±(m_+^{(1)} + m_+^{(2)} + 1), ±(m_+^{(1)} − m_+^{(2)})} if N_2^{an} = 1, and {±(m_+^{(1)} + m_+^{(2)} + ½), ±(m_+^{(1)} − m_+^{(2)} + ½)} otherwise. Hence ⌊s_π(ρ)²⌋ + ⌊s_π(ρ')²⌋ = a_+^{(1)} + a_+^{(2)} if N_2^{an} = 1, and = (m_+^{(1)} + m_+^{(2)} + ½)² + (m_+^{(1)} − m_+^{(2)} + ½)² − ½ = a_+^{(1)} + a_+^{(2)} − 1 otherwise.

Arithmetic checked for both branches.

items.name: Ramified unitary case, Q = X + 1
items.statement: In the situation of §8.2 with Q(X) = X + 1: f_1 = 2m_−^{(1)}, and the reducibility points are {±(m_−^{(1)} + m_−^{(2)} + ½), ±(m_−^{(1)} − m_−^{(2)} − ½)} if N_2^{an} = 1, and {±(m_−^{(1)} ± m_−^{(2)})} otherwise. In both cases ⌊s_π(ρ)²⌋ + ⌊s_π(ρ')²⌋ = a_−^{(1)} + a_−^{(2)}.

items.name: (8.1) for ramified unitary groups
items.statement: Σ_P a_P^{(1)} deg(P) = 2N_1 + 1, and Σ_P a_P^{(2)} deg(P) = 2N_2 if N_2^{an} = 1, = 2N_2 + N_2^{an} otherwise; summing over all depth zero self-dual irreducible cuspidal representations of all GL_n(F), equation (8.1) is satisfied.

Totals: 2N + 1 if N_2^{an} = 1, and 2N + N_2^{an} otherwise (the −1 of the X − 1 case cancels the +1), i.e. dim V = N_Ĝ.

items.name: (8.1) for special orthogonal groups (sketched)
items.statement: The case of special orthogonal groups is exactly analogous; one checks (8.1) by working through the cases according to the parities of N_1^{an}, N_2^{an}. For example, if both are odd, then with Q(X) = X ± 1, ⌊s_π(ρ)²⌋ + ⌊s_π(ρ')²⌋ = a_±^{(1)} + a_±^{(2)} + 1; the extra 1's compensate for the dual groups of 𝒢^{(i)}_{N_i} acting on spaces of dimension 2N_i = 2N_i + N_i^{an} − 1.

Details not given in the paper (the special orthogonal and ramified unitary cases are only sketched).

items.name: Equality (8.1) and half-integrality
items.statement: Let π be a depth zero irreducible cuspidal representation of a classical group G (symplectic, special orthogonal, unitary). Then Σ_{ρ ∈ 𝒜^σ_{[0]}(F)} ⌊(s_π(ρ))²⌋ n_ρ = N_Ĝ (8.1), where N_Ĝ is the dimension of the natural representation of Ĝ; and s_π(ρ) ∈ ½ℤ for all ρ ∈ 𝒜^σ_{[0]}(F).

This is Theorem (i) of the introduction restricted to depth zero ρ; together with the next item it gives the inequality ⩾ in (1.3).

items.name: Lower bound in (1.3)
items.statement: For π as above, Σ_{ρ ∈ 𝒜^σ(F)} ⌊(s_π(ρ))²⌋ n_ρ ⩾ N_Ĝ.

Immediate from (8.1) since all terms are ⩾ 0. Equality (1.3) needs the vanishing of positive depth contributions (next item).

items.name: Cited: positive depth ρ do not contribute
items.statement: For ρ a positive depth self-dual irreducible cuspidal representation (and π depth zero cuspidal), s_π(ρ) ∈ {0, ±½}, so these ρ do not contribute to the sum in (1.3). Alternatively, in many cases the opposite inequality Σ ⌊s_π(ρ)²⌋ n_ρ ⩽ N_Ĝ was proved by Mœglin [38].

Not proved here: 'the techniques used here, together with the results in [36] (Miyauchi–Stevens semisimple types), easily show' it, with details deferred to [6] (Blondel–Henniart–Stevens, in preparation). Mœglin [38] (reducibility points for induced cuspidals) gives the upper bound 'in many cases'.

items.name: Expected Langlands parameter from the Jordan set (cited expectation)
items.statement: Let ϕ : W_F × SL_2(ℂ) → Ĝ ⋊ W_F be a Langlands parameter for G whose L-packet Π_ϕ contains an irreducible cuspidal representation π. Then one should have ϕ = ⊕_{(ρ,m) ∈ Jord(π)} ϕ_ρ ⊗ st_m, where ϕ_ρ is the irreducible representation of W_F corresponding to ρ under the Langlands correspondence for general linear groups and st_m is the m-dimensional irreducible representation of SL_2(ℂ).
items.note: Expectation, known for quasi-split G by Mœglin [41] (via Arthur [2], Mok [43]). The LLC for GL_n that defines ϕ_ρ is planned in ET.6 ('Construct the characteristic-zero local correspondence for GL_m(E), E a finite extension of Q_p, with full Frobenius-semisimple Weil–Deligne parameters'); packets for classical groups are only a source-owner task in ML.4 ('Give Arthur/Mok/KMSW classification inputs explicit proof-source owners: ... packets'). Mœglin's Jordan-set description itself is in no stage.

items.name: Expected size of the L-packet
items.statement: With ℓ(π) = #Jord(π), the number of representations one expects in the packet Π_ϕ is 2^{ℓ(π)−1}, the number of characters of the component group of Cent_Ĝ(Im(ϕ)) trivial on the centre of Ĝ.

Expectation from the local Langlands conjecture/Arthur's classification; cf. ML.4 (source-owner task only). Used only for discussion (Examples 9.3 onward).

items.name: E(π), e(π), e_0(π)
items.statement: E(π) = {ρ ∈ 𝒜^σ(F) : s_π(ρ) is a positive integer} and e(π) = #E(π); this is the number of ρ ∈ 𝒜^σ(F) such that (ρ, m) ∈ Jord(π) for some odd integer m. e_0(π) = 1 if s_π(ρ) is an odd positive integer for some ρ ∈ 𝒜^σ(F), and 0 otherwise.

The convention for ℕ is inconsistent between E(π) and e_0(π) (PAPER-LUST-STEVENS-20/E25); the intended meaning is s_π(ρ) ∈ ℤ_{⩾1} for E(π) and s_π(ρ) an odd positive integer for e_0(π). Printed as s_π(ρ) ∈ ℕ and s_π(ρ) ∈ 1 + 2ℕ, which cannot both be meant with one convention for ℕ (PAPER-LUST-STEVENS-20/E25).

items.name: Expected number of cuspidals in a packet (Mœglin)
items.statement: The number of irreducible cuspidal representations one expects in the L-packet Π_ϕ is 2^{e(π)−e_0(π)}, the number of characters of the component group of Cent_Ĝ(Im(ϕ)) which are trivial on the centre of Ĝ and alternating in the sense of [40, Section 8].

Mœglin's characterisation of cuspidal members by alternating characters: proved in [40, §8] for unitary groups; holds for quasi-split unitary, orthogonal, symplectic and GSpin groups by [39]. Assumed in general as (A).

items.name: Assumption (A)
items.statement: (A) The description of the number of irreducible cuspidal representation[s] in an L-packet above (2^{e(π)−e_0(π)}) is valid for the group G. Extra care is needed when G is an even-dimensional special orthogonal group (Example 9.6).

Not needed for the results on inertial reducibility sets, only for their interpretation as unions of L-packets.

items.name: Inertial reducibility multiset IRed(π)
items.statement: IRed(π) = {{([ρ], m) : ρ ∈ 𝒜^σ(F), m ∈ ℕ with 2s_π(ρ) = m + 1}}, where [ρ] denotes the inertial equivalence class of ρ (the set of unramified twists of ρ).

Note that the Examples list ([ρ], s_π(ρ)) instead of ([ρ], m) (PAPER-LUST-STEVENS-20/E26).

items.name: Recovering {m_P^{(1)}, m_P^{(2)}} from reducibility points, generic P
items.statement: For each irreducible k_F/k_o-self-dual monic P ∈ k_F[X] with P(X) ≠ X ± 1 or k_F ≠ k_o, and ρ = ρ_P ∈ 𝒜^σ_{[0]}(F) with associated characteristic polynomial P and ρ' its self-dual unramified twist: {m_P^{(1)}, m_P^{(2)}} = {⌊|s_π(ρ) ± s_π(ρ')|_∞⌋}.

Checked from the §8 formulas: the two values are max + ½ and min + ½.

items.name: Recovering {m_P^{(1)}, m_P^{(2)}} from reducibility points, P = X ± 1
items.statement: If P(X) = X ± 1 and k_F = k_o, so that ρ is a character of GL_1(F) of order at most 2, then {m_P^{(1)}, m_P^{(2)}} = {⌊|s_π(ρ) ± s_π(ρ')|_∞ / 2⌋}.

Checked against §§8.1–8.2 formulas.

items.name: Cuspidals with the same inertial reducibility set
items.statement: One obtains the same inertial reducibility set as for π only for irreducible cuspidal representations π' (of depth zero) with {m_P^{(1)}(π), m_P^{(2)}(π)} = {m_P^{(1)}(π'), m_P^{(2)}(π')} for every irreducible k_F/k_o-self-dual monic polynomial P ∈ k_F[X]. Hence, to obtain other representations with the same inertial reducibility set it is enough to exchange (some of) the integers m_P^{(1)}(π), m_P^{(2)}(π), though this is not always possible for parity reasons.

This is Theorem (iii) of the introduction in its first form.

items.name: Q(π) and q(π)
items.statement: Q(π) = {irreducible self-dual monic P ∈ k_F[X] : m_P^{(1)}(π) ≠ m_P^{(2)}(π)} and q(π) := #Q(π).

items.name: Remark 9.2: integrality of one reducibility point
items.statement: If P ∈ k_F[X] is an irreducible k_F/k_o-self-dual monic polynomial with P(X) ≠ X ± 1 or k_F ≠ k_o, and ρ_P, ρ'_P are the corresponding self-dual irreducible cuspidal representations of some GL_n(F), then one of s_π(ρ_P), s_π(ρ'_P) is integral and the other non-integral. In particular (exactly) one of ρ_P, ρ'_P is in E(π) if and only if P ∈ Q(π).

Checked: the integral point is ⩾ 1 iff m_P^{(1)} ≠ m_P^{(2)}.

items.name: Parametrisation by maps ε : Q(π) → {1,2}
items.statement: The irreducible cuspidals π' with IRed(π') = IRed(π) are parametrized by maps ε : Q(π) → {1, 2} (not all such maps are permissible, and each map may give rise to more than one representation); extend ε by ε(P) = 1 for P ∉ Q(π) and put m_P^{(i)}(ε) = m_P^{(i·ε(P))}, the index understood modulo 3.

items.name: Symplectic groups: the 2^{q(π)+δ(π)} cuspidals with the same IRed
items.statement: Let G = Sp_{2N}(F); there are no restrictions on the maps ε : Q(π) → {1, 2}. For each ε there are, for i = 1, 2, semisimple elements s_ε^{(i)} in suitable odd special orthogonal groups SO_{2N'_i+1}(k_F) with characteristic polynomial ∏_P P(X)^{a_P^{(i)}(ε)}, where a_P^{(i)}(ε) are related to m_P^{(i)}(ε) = m_P^{(i·ε(P))} as in (7.2). Correspondingly there are irreducible cuspidal representations τ_ε = τ_ε^{(1)} ⊗ τ_ε^{(2)} of 𝒢_{N'_1,N'_2} = Sp_{2N'_1}(k_F) × Sp_{2N'_2}(k_F), 2^{δ(π)} of them for each ε. Inflating each τ_ε to J_{N'_1,N'_2} and inducing to G gives an irreducible cuspidal representation; thus one gets 2^{q(π)+δ(π)} irreducible cuspidal representations of G (with the same inertial reducibility set as π).

Uses Lusztig's classification (7.2) (existence of s_ε and the count 2 of cuspidals in ℰ(Sp, s) when the −1-eigenspace is nonzero) and Morris's depth-zero construction (irreducibility of compact induction).

items.name: Symplectic groups: e(π) and e_0(π)
items.statement: For G symplectic: e(π) = q(π) + δ(π) + 1 if δ(π) ⩽ 1, and e(π) = q(π) + δ(π) if δ(π) = 2. Moreover e_0(π) = 1 always, since either s_π(𝟏) or s_π(ω_0) is an odd integer (𝟏 the trivial character of GL_1(F), ω_0 the unramified character of order two).

Derived from Remark 9.2 and the X ± 1 formulas of §8.1; counting checked case by case. Relies on 1 ∈ 1 + 2ℕ.

items.name: Symplectic groups: one or two L-packets
items.statement: Assuming (A), the 2^{q(π)+δ(π)} representations constructed are the irreducible cuspidal representations in a union of two L-packets if δ(π) = 2, and in a single L-packet otherwise.

Compare 2^{q+δ} with 2^{e−e_0}. This is the precise form of the intro Theorem for symplectic groups (Π_ϕ ∪ Π_ϕ').

items.name: Example 9.3 (Sp_6, a single L-packet)
items.statement: G = Sp_6(F), J_{2,1} with reductive quotient 𝒢_{2,1} ≃ Sp_4(k_F) × SL_2(k_F); θ_10 the unique cuspidal in ℰ(Sp_4(k_F), 1) (characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^5), τ an irreducible cuspidal of SL_2(k_F) in a Lusztig series with characteristic polynomial (X − 1)(X + 1)² (dimension (q−1)/2, two such); π = c-Ind_{J_{2,1}}^G λ_π with λ_π inflated from θ_10 ⊗ τ. Then s_π(ρ) ∈ {0, ½} unless ρ is a character of GL_1(F); m_{X−1}^{(1)} = 1, m_{X−1}^{(2)} = 0, m_{X+1}^{(1)} = 0, m_{X+1}^{(2)} = 1; {s_π(𝟏), s_π(ω_0)} = {2, 1}, {s_π(ω_1), s_π(ω_2)} = {1}; IRed(π) = {{([𝟏],3), ([𝟏],1), ([ω_1],1), ([ω_1],1)}} (printed with the values of s_π in place of m; E26); ϕ_π = 𝟏 ⊗ (st_3 ⊕ st_1) ⊕ ω_0 ⊕ ω_1 ⊕ ω_2; E(π) = {𝟏, ω_0, ω_1, ω_2}, e(π) = 4; the L-packet has 16 members, 8 cuspidal; Q(π) = {X + 1, X − 1}, q(π) = 2, δ(π) = 1; the 8 cuspidals are the inductions of θ_10 ⊗ τ, θ_10 ⊗ τ' from J_{2,1} or J_{1,2}, and of τ_1, τ'_1 ∈ ℰ(Sp_6(k_F), s_1) (s_1 ∈ SO_7(k_F) with characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^5(X + 1)²) from J_{3,0} or J_{0,3}.

items.name: Example 9.4 (Sp_4, union of two L-packets)
items.statement: G = Sp_4(F), J_{1,1} with 𝒢_{1,1} ≃ SL_2(k_F) × SL_2(k_F); τ_1, τ_2 cuspidals of SL_2(k_F) each in a Lusztig series with characteristic polynomial (X − 1)(X + 1)²; π = c-Ind_{J_{1,1}}^G λ_π. Then IRed(π) = {{([𝟏],1), ([ω_1],3)}} (printed as {{([𝟏],1), ([ω_1],2)}}, the values of s_π; E26) and (9.5) ϕ_π = 𝟏 ⊕ ω ⊗ (st_3 ⊕ st_1) with ω ∈ {ω_1, ω_2} not determined, reflecting m_{X+1}^{(1)} = m_{X+1}^{(2)} = 1, δ(π) = 2. The 4 cuspidals in the union of the two L-packets (ω = ω_1, ω_2) are obtained by independently choosing each τ_i among the two cuspidals of SL_2(k_F) of dimension (q−1)/2.

items.name: Unramified unitary groups: parity of deg P^{a_P}
items.statement: Let G be an unramified unitary group of dimension 2N + N^{an}, π induced from τ_π^{(1)} ⊗ τ_π^{(2)} of 𝒢^{(1)}_{N_1} × 𝒢^{(2)}_{N_2}, 𝒢^{(i)}_{N_i} = U(V̄_{(i)}), dim V̄_{(i)} = 2N_i + N_i^{an}. For another maximal parahoric with reductive quotient 𝒢^{(1)}_{N'_1} × 𝒢^{(2)}_{N'_2}, dim V̄'_{(i)} ≡ dim V̄_{(i)} (mod 2). With a_P^{(i)} = ½ m_P^{(i)}(m_P^{(i)} + 1) and deg P odd, deg(P(X)^{a_P^{(i)}}) is odd if m_P^{(i)} ≡ 1, 2 (mod 4) and even if m_P^{(i)} ≡ 0, 3 (mod 4). Hence if one m_P^{(i)} is 1, 2 (mod 4) and the other 0, 3 (mod 4), m_P^{(1)} cannot be exchanged with m_P^{(2)} independently of other changes.

items.name: Unramified unitary: IRed-class is exactly one L-packet
items.statement: For ε : Q(π) → {1, 2} with #{P ∈ Q_0(π) : ε(P) = 2} even (ε(P) = 1 for P ∉ Q(π)), there are semisimple s_ε^{(i)} in suitable U(2N'_i + N_i^{an}, k_F) with characteristic polynomial ∏_P P(X)^{a_P^{(i)}(ε)}, a_P^{(i)}(ε) = ½ m_P^{(i)}(ε)(m_P^{(i)}(ε) + 1), m_P^{(i)}(ε) = m_P^{(i·ε(P))} (index mod 3); correspondingly a unique irreducible cuspidal τ_ε = τ_ε^{(1)} ⊗ τ_ε^{(2)} of 𝒢_{N'_1,N'_2} and, by inflation and compact induction, a unique irreducible cuspidal representation of G. This yields 2^{q(π)−e_0(π)} inequivalent irreducible cuspidal representations with the same inertial reducibility set as π, exactly the number of cuspidals in the L-packet of π.

items.name: Example 9.6 (split SO_8: half a packet for SO, a full one for O)
items.statement: G = SO(V), dim V = 8, Witt index 4; J_{4,0}, J_{0,4} with reductive quotients SO_8^+(k_F); τ the unipotent cuspidal of SO_8^+(k_F); π = c-Ind_{J_{4,0}}^G τ, π' = c-Ind_{J_{0,4}}^G τ. IRed(π) = IRed(π') = {{([𝟏],3), ([𝟏],3)}} (printed with the values of s_π; E26), ϕ_π = ϕ_π' = 𝟏 ⊗ (st_3 ⊕ st_1) ⊕ ω_0 ⊗ (st_3 ⊕ st_1). The packet should contain four cuspidals but π, π' are the only two with this IRed. By Proposition 7.9(ii), τ extends in two ways to O_8^+(k_F); inducing the inflations from J^+_{4,0}, J^+_{0,4} to G^+ = O(V) gives four inequivalent irreducible cuspidals, two restricting to π and two to π'. So for even orthogonal groups the expected number should be interpreted for the full orthogonal group.

items.name: Example 9.7 (SO_5: union of four L-packets)
items.statement: G = SO(V), dim V = 5, Witt index 2; J_{2,0} with 𝒢°_{2,0} ≃ SO_4^+(k_F) × SO_1(k_F). There is s in the dual of SO_4^+(k_F) with characteristic polynomial (X − 1)²(X + 1)² such that ℰ(SO_4^+(k_F), s) contains a cuspidal τ (two such). items.name: Example 9.8 (SO_20, two inner forms)
items.statement: G = SO(V), dim V = 20, Witt index 8, anisotropic part of dimension 4; J_{4,4} with 𝒢°_{4,4} ≃ SO^−_{10}(k_F) × SO^−_{10}(k_F); s_1, s_2 in the dual of SO^−_{10}(k_F) with characteristic polynomials (X − 1)^8(X + 1)² and (X − 1)²(X + 1)^8, cuspidal τ_i ∈ ℰ(SO^−_{10}(k_F), s_i) (two each); λ_π inflated from one of two extensions of τ_1 ⊗ τ_2 to 𝒢_{4,4}; π = c-Ind_{J_{4,4}}^G λ_π. routes.title: Smooth representations of local groups, Part II: types, depth and the construction of supercuspidal representations
routes.brief: This route coalesces with SmoothRepresentationsPartII, proposed by PAPER-FINTZEN-21 and joined by PAPER-BUSHNELL-HENNIART-17, PAPER-NEWTON-THORNE-21 and PAPER-GAN-HARRIS-SAWIN-ETAL-24; keep its id, title, parent, area and brief. Lust–Stevens (arXiv:1611.08421; Proc. LMS 121 (2020)) add the depth-zero theory of classical groups over a p-adic field F with p odd: G symplectic, special orthogonal or unitary (F/F_o quadratic), defined by an ε-hermitian form. Final theorems, as the version of record states them (Introduction, p. 1086; arXiv v1 §1, p. 4): for π a depth-zero irreducible cuspidal representation of G, (i) Σ_{ρ∈𝒜^σ(F)} ⌊s_π(ρ)²⌋ n_ρ ⩾ N_Ĝ, the sum over depth-zero ρ being exactly N_Ĝ (8.1), where s_π(ρ) is the reducibility point of Ind ρ|det|^s ⊗ π (arXiv v1 claims the equality (1.3); see E33); (ii) the multiset IRed(π) of inertial reducibility data is computed explicitly from the data (P, τ) with π = c-Ind_{P}^{G} τ; (iii) the cuspidal π′ with IRed(π′) = IRed(π) are described explicitly, and their number is the expected number in one, two or four L-packets, or half the expected number in one packet for an even special orthogonal G (§9.3, Example 9.6; E34). For G symplectic the theorem gives the cuspidal members of Π_φ ∪ Π_φ′ for a tame parameter φ. The roadmap must cover: the lattice-function model of parahoric subgroups of classical groups and their reductive quotients; Morris's classification of depth-zero cuspidals by compact induction from maximal parahorics (excluding the split SO(1,1) ≅ GL_1, whose depth-zero cuspidals are characters of F^×: the compact-normalizer statement, compact induction and the injectivity of lattice labels all fail there, E7, so that case is treated separately or deferred); Silberger's reducibility theorem and Blondel's formula relating reducibility points to the parameters of the Hecke algebra of a Bushnell–Kutzko cover (Miyauchi–Stevens covers); the reduction to finite Hecke algebras of the reductive quotients (§6); the synthesis of §8 from the finite parameters f_τ; and the §9 counting of L-packet sizes. The finite-group computation of §7 (Lusztig series and the Jordan decomposition for finite classical and similitude groups, the parameters f_τ, the SO-to-O extension) is routed to ModularRepresentationsOfFiniteReductiveGroups (route 2): import it, do not build it here. Import, never re-plan: SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups SR.1–SR.3 (Hecke algebras, compact induction and Jacquet functors, Bernstein subcategories); Bushnell–Kutzko types and covers from this Part II's own Fintzen layers; buildings and parahoric group schemes from ReductiveGroupsPartII RG2.2–RG2.3; finite classical groups, Lusztig's classification of their cuspidal representations and the finite Hecke parameters f_τ from ModularRepresentationsOfFiniteReductiveGroups (route 2); Witt theory of quadratic forms from the Tau Ceti QuadraticFormInvariants roadmap (layer 1) and its hermitian variants from GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.2; the local Langlands correspondence for GL_m from EndoscopicTransferAndUnitaryTraceComparison ET.6; Arthur/Mœglin packets for classical groups only as statements from ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.4. Mœglin's result that Jord(π) determines the parameter (1.1) is an input, stated with its quasi-split hypothesis; equality (1.3) in general depends on Mœglin and on the vanishing of positive-depth contributions (arXiv [6], "in preparation"; printed Remark 8.2 leaves the details as an exercise), which the roadmap must record as a dependency, not assume. Fixes by FIX-RT-PAPER-LUST-STEVENS-20: the reductive quotient J/J^1 carries the determinant condition only when F = F_o or F/F_o is unramified, and is the full U(V̄_(1)) × U(V̄_(2)) in the ramified case (E5); J° is maximal unless a residual factor is the split SO(1,1,k_F) and G is not itself two-dimensional special orthogonal (E6); the normalizer, compact-induction and lattice-label uniqueness statements assume G is not split SO(1,1) (E7).
routes.reason: Nothing in the atlas plans depth-zero types, covers and reducibility points for classical groups, or L-packet counting, and the maintainer's note asks for a Part II of SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups for what it lacks. SmoothRepresentationsPartII is the existing Part II in exactly this direction (types, depth and the construction of supercuspidals), already joined by four papers, so this route joins it with byte-identical id, parent, title and area (PROTOCOL.md §15) rather than proposing a rival Part II. The review moved the finite-group items of §§3, 6 and 7 to route 2: that Part II's accepted brief (PAPER-FINTZEN-21) says no Deligne–Lusztig classification is required there, and the atlas already has one owner for Deligne–Lusztig theory.

routes.title: Reductive algebraic groups, Part II: modular representations and generic GL3 lattices
routes.brief: This route coalesces with ModularRepresentationsOfFiniteReductiveGroups, the Part II of Tau Ceti's Reductive algebraic groups roadmap proposed by PAPER-LE-LEHUNG-LEVIN-ETAL-20 (route accepted) and reused by PAPER-LE-LEHUNG-LEVIN-ETAL-23. Keep its id, parent, title and area, and its rule of one foundation for Deligne–Lusztig theory. Lust–Stevens §7 (arXiv:1611.08421v1, pp. 13–24; Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 121 (2020) 1083–1120, pp. 1096–1107) add the characteristic-zero Harish-Chandra theory of finite classical groups in odd characteristic, which their depth-zero p-adic results consume. Final results, as the paper states them (arXiv numbering; in print, Lemma 7.3 is Lusztig's [32, Lemma 8.9] and each subsequent number goes up by one). Lemma 7.3: for 𝒢 = Sp_{2N} or SO^±_{2N} inside its similitude group 𝒢̃ (connected centre), a cuspidal π ∈ ℰ(𝒢^F, s) extends to an irreducible representation in ℰ(𝒢̃^F, s̃) iff 𝒢*_s is connected iff at most one of ±1 is an eigenvalue of s. sourceIssues.printed: The source claims any pair of these elements anticommutes because r is odd, and each squares to 0. It argues that the v_i are isotropic except when ζ_i = −1, and that not all ζ_i can be −1 because their product is 1 with r odd. It concludes that every a ∈ A^1 commuting with s has a^2 = 0 and hence is non-invertible.
sourceIssues.correction: The claim that every a ∈ A^1 commuting with s̃ has a^2 = 0 is false; a different argument is needed that no element of C^1(𝒱) centralizes s̃ when 1 is not an eigenvalue of s (e.g. via the image of such an element in O(𝒱) ∖ SO(𝒱), which forces −1 to be an eigenvalue, and then a separate analysis of the (−1)-eigenspace, whose volume element anticommutes with its odd part). Also 'commutes with s' should read s̃.
sourceIssues.reason: Counterexample to the intermediate claims: q ≡ 1 mod 3, ζ a primitive cube root of unity, 𝒱 six-dimensional split with s = diag(ζ,ζ,ζ,ζ^{−1},ζ^{−1},ζ^{−1}) on eigenvectors x_1,x_2,x_3 (eigenvalue ζ) and y_1,y_2,y_3 (eigenvalue ζ^{−1}), B(x_i,y_j) = δ_ij/2. Then x_1x_2x_3 and y_1y_2y_3 are admissible monomials (product of eigenvalues 1, r = 3), but in the fermionic model (x_i ↦ creation, y_i ↦ annihilation) a = x_1x_2x_3 + y_1y_2y_3 has a^2 = −(n_1n_2n_3 + (1−n_1)(1−n_2)(1−n_3)) ≠ 0, so the monomials do not anticommute and a^2 ≠ 0. (Monomials sharing a factor, e.g. v_1v_2v_3 and v_1v_4v_5 with orthogonal vectors, even commute.) In this example a is still non-invertible and the stated conclusion of the paragraph (no element of C^1(𝒱) centralizes s̃) is expected to hold (for s^2 = 1 it is in [32, Lemma 8.9]), so Proposition 7.9 is plausibly true, but the argument as written is invalid.

sourceIssues.printed: The source writes V = ⊕_P V_P ⊕ V_0 for the rational eigenspace decomposition associated with monic, irreducible, self-dual polynomials of even degree. sourceIssues.correction: Let L* be the minimal F-stable Levi subgroup containing the centralizer of s (the Levi of a parabolic that need not be F-stable); with V_0 = ker(s² − 1), L* = G*_s whenever s|_{V_0} = ±1, and L is a product of general linear groups with twisted Frobenius and a classical group G_0 with connected centre.
